title: Magna Carta
subject: histoire
description: In June 1215, John Lackland set his seal to a charter forced on him by his barons. Over the centuries, a feudal text became the symbol of law standing above the king.

hero.hook: A cornered king signs. Eight centuries later, the whole world is still talking about it.

blocks.text: In June **1215**, in the meadow of **Runnymede**, near London, King **John Lackland** of England set his seal to the **Magna Carta**, the “Great Charter.” It was not a gesture of generosity. It was a trial of strength: the barons, the great lords of the kingdom, wanted to break the king's arbitrary rule.
The text was drawn up to head off a civil war. As an immediate settlement it failed. Yet it slowly became the symbol of an explosive idea: even the king is under the law.

King since **1199**, John lurched from one disaster to the next. Against the French king [[Philip II Augustus]], he suffered the [[loss of Normandy (1204)]]. To win his lands back, he squeezed the [[feudal system]]: the king granted land in return for loyalty and military service, but John piled up taxes, hostages, and arbitrary fines. The customs that bound him to his vassals fell apart.

His quarrel with Pope [[Innocent III]] left him more isolated still. After the defeat at [[Bouvines]] (**1214**), where Philip Augustus beat a coalition that included England, the barons rebelled and seized London. John had no choice left: negotiate, or lose the crown.
The nickname “Lackland” has nothing to do with his French defeats. As the youngest son of Henry II, he simply received no lands of his own at birth.

On **June 15, 1215**, the two sides met at Runnymede. Shaped by the archbishop of Canterbury [[Stephen Langton]], the document ran to **63 clauses**. Two of them changed everything. **Clause 39**: no free man may be arrested without a judgment by his peers. **Clause 40**: the king may neither sell nor delay justice.

blocks.caption: The Magna Carta of 1215, a parchment that became a political myth

blocks.text: This was not democracy yet. The charter speaks above all to “free men,” not to serfs, the peasants tied to the land. It is first of all a peace treaty between a king and his barons. But the idea was set down: power has written limits.

By August, John had the pope annul the text. Civil war started again. The charter survived thanks to the king's death in **1216**: the young **Henry III** reissued it to calm the kingdom. Confirmed again and again, it entered English law.
There is no single original from 1215, but several copies sent out to the counties. Only four have survived.

In the 17th century, lawyers such as [[Edward Coke]] brought it out again against the absolutism of the Stuarts, kings who wanted to rule without limits. A medieval parchment became the claimed ancestor of parliamentary liberties.

events.title: Reissue
events.detail: Henry III saved the text to steady the throne.

blocks.text: British colonists carried the charter to America. The Founding Fathers drew on it for the [[Bill of Rights]], the first amendments to the American Constitution. [[Habeas corpus]], the principle that forbids arbitrary arrest, carries clause 39 forward. In **1948**, [[Eleanor Roosevelt]] saw in it a “Great Charter” for all of humanity.
Today only three clauses are still in force in England. That hardly matters. Magna Carta counts less as living law than as a symbol: nobody stands above the law.
Wrung out of John Lackland in **1215**, Magna Carta states that the king too is under the law. Out of a treaty between barons and king came one of the founding myths of modern liberty.
